Before a Medical Emergency, Save Your Out-of-Pocket Maximum and Sign a Health Care Proxy

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Get ready for a medical emergency while you’re healthy.
  • A heart attack or bad car crash can run up hospital bills while you’re too sick to speak for yourself.
  • Most health intends cap your share of those bills at an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a plan year for covered in-network care.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get ready for a medical emergency while you’re healthy. Keep savings equal to your health plan’s out-of-pocket maximum, and make sure disability coverage would replace part of your paycheck. Then sign a health care proxy and a HIPAA release so someone you trust can talk to your doctors and decide for you.

A heart attack or bad car crash can run up hospital bills while you’re too sick to speak for yourself.

Most health intends cap your share of those bills at an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a plan year for covered in-network care. It’s on page one of your plan’s Summary of Benefits and Coverage, called the out-of-pocket limit. Save that much.

Say a married couple’s family blueprint caps their share at $9,000 a year. They keep $9,000 in a health savings account, and each has signed a health care proxy naming the other to make medical decisions. When one has a heart attack, the account pays their share, and the proxy settles who decides. Without one, state law would usually pick the spouse, but a relative could contest that in court.

Keep that money in a health savings account if your proposal qualifies, since the balance carries over and withdrawals for qualified medical bills are tax-free. If not, build it into your emergency fund with automatic deposits each payday. If illness keeps you out of work for months, disability insurance through your job or your own policy replaces part of your pay.

Recent findings suggest that sign your own proxy, also called a health care power of attorney, and a living will, which tells doctors what treatment you’d want if you can’t decide for yourself. One form, an advance directive, usually covers both. Add a HIPAA release, which names who can get your medical information, since some providers want permission in writing. Keep copies, with a list of your medications and doctors, where family can find them.

After a serious diagnosis, ask your insurer whether it offers a case manager, usually a nurse or social worker, to help coordinate your care. Nonprofit hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy, which can mean free or discounted care, so ask for the application before the first bill.

Start with the forms, since they cost little or nothing. CaringInfo posts every state’s advance directive form free, and you don’t need a lawyer. Give copies to the person you name and your doctor.

Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

📅 20 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives.
  • Recent findings suggest that A health sharing initiative (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance company.
  • Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing aims have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

Recent findings suggest that A health sharing initiative (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance company. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA prepares, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

Sources indicate that traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace plan, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health strategy with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

In a recent development, employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace looks are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing prepares aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

Recent findings suggest that it works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing initiative and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing blueprint cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

It has been revealed that changing only your travel days can cut the fare. Google’s analysis of five years of its flight data found that leaving on a Monday and returning on a Tuesday or Wednesday costs about 14% less than flying on the weekend.

Recent findings suggest that on Google Flights, open the date grid or price graph to see which travel dates around your trip have the lowest fares. Add every airport within an easy drive to the search, since a smaller airport nearby can be cheaper than your closest one. Also compare the round-trip fare with two one-way tickets on different airlines.

Recent findings suggest that say a family of four moves its departure from Saturday to Tuesday and flies from a smaller airport 40 minutes away, and each round-trip ticket costs $90 less. That’s $360 saved, minus gas for the longer drive.

In a recent development, then turn on price tracking for the route, so Google emails you when the price changes significantly. Google’s analysis found domestic fares low from 22 to 57 days before departure and cheapest around 39 days out. International fares were low from 50 to 133 days out. For Thanksgiving or Christmas, book holiday flights in October instead of waiting for a sale.

Before you compare a basic economy or budget airline fare with a regular one, add the extras you’ll pay for. Basic economy, an airline’s most restricted ticket, usually limits bags and comes without a seat assignment. Google Flights’ bags filter adds checked or carry-on bag fees to the prices it demonstrates. Add the cost of choosing a seat for each traveler who needs one.

Industry observers note that book the lowest total on the airline’s own site. The Transportation Department’s 24-hour rule covers tickets bought at least seven days before departure. Under it, the airline must either give a full refund on a ticket canceled within 24 hours or hold the fare for 24 hours without payment. Tickets bought through travel booking sites and agents aren’t covered.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plenty of jobs pay you to walk, lift, and climb instead of sitting, and some pay well above the typical U.S. wage. Before you switch, compare each job’s pay and training with what it asks of your body, since the active jobs you can start fastest tend to pay the least.

Sources indicate that picture an office worker who trades her desk for a mail route. She now spends most of her shift on her feet, and the exercise she used to pay a gym for comes with the job.

Industry observers note that the difference shows up in calories. The Compendium of Physical Activities, a research list rating how much energy activities take, scores each one against sitting quietly, which burns about 1 calorie an hour for every 2.2 pounds you weigh. For a 160-pound person, that puts an hour of office work at about 110 calories, delivering mail on foot at about 170, general yard work at about 290, and firefighting at about 580.

Industry observers note that carriers on walking routes cover about 4 to 12 miles a day and spend up to about six hours on foot, the National Association of Letter Carriers says. Over those six hours, a 160-pound carrier burns roughly 350 more calories than she would at a desk. The 15 jobs below run from that kind of steady walking to heavy lifting, and their pay ranges just as widely.

Pay below is each job’s May 2025 median from the Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), meaning half of workers in the job earn more and half less. For comparison, the median for all U.S. workers was $50,980.

In a recent development, the quickest jobs to start mostly pay the least. Animal care, grounds work, material moving, construction labor, and fitness training take little or no schooling, and all five pay under the $50,980 national median. Mail carriers are the exception. The other better-paid jobs here typically start with a training program, a degree, or an apprenticeship.

Industry observers note that physical work also brings more injuries than a desk job. BLS counts construction laborers, material movers, and flight attendants among the occupations with the highest injury and illness rates, and nurses and therapist assistants who lift patients are prone to back injuries.

The strain adds up with age. A University of Michigan Retirement and Disability Research Center study found that workers in more physically demanding jobs are more likely to be retired at any given age. The effect showed up almost entirely in men and was larger among those without a college degree. That makes saving early matter more in a heavy job, since your working years may be fewer.

To earn while you train, start with the trades. Electricians and elevator installers learn through apprenticeships that pay for their hours on the job, and carpenters can train the same way. The Labor Department’s Apprenticeship Finder lets you search openings by career and location.

In a recent development, the easy version of a city weekend, a downtown hotel with the car in its garage and a ticket to every substantial attraction, is also the priciest. In the Loop, Chicago’s downtown, the Palmer House Hilton charges $57 a night just to self-park.

Good transit means you need neither a car nor a downtown room. A hotel near a train or bus stop a few miles out often costs less than one downtown, and so can a hostel’s private room.

Two other savings need a check before you count on them. A museum’s free day may be for local residents only, and an attractions pass saves money only on places you’d have paid to see anyway.

In Chicago, a CTA 3-day pass costs $15 and covers 72 hours of buses and trains, including the Blue Line ride from O’Hare that costs $5 without a pass. Buy it from a vending machine in the O’Hare station. A taxi from O’Hare to downtown averages $50, the airport says. Stay near a Blue Line stop such as Logan Square, and the same train takes you to the Loop.

Industry observers note that the Art Institute, the Field Museum, and the Shedd Aquarium save their free days for Illinois residents. Lincoln Park Zoo and the National Museum of Mexican Art are free to everyone, and Chicago Greeter volunteers lead free hour-long walks from the Chicago Cultural Center.

According to recent reports, chicago CityPASS costs $144 per adult for five attractions over nine days, with upgrades such as faster entry at several of them. See just three, such as the Skydeck, the Art Institute, and the Field Museum, and general admission without the upgrades starts at $94 for all three, $50 less than the pass.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that inflation, the steady rise in prices, shrinks what each dollar you hold in cash can buy, even at the modest pace the Federal Reserve aims for. Keep your emergency fund and money you’ll spend within five years in savings, and invest the rest, since stocks have grown faster than prices over long periods.

Industry observers note that the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% a year over the long run, and even that pace doubles prices in about 35 years, so a dollar kept in cash buys half as much. In the 12 months through June 2022, prices rose 9.1%, the biggest jump in 40 years, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Prices climb when spending outruns what businesses can supply, or when costs like energy and wages rise and get passed on to shoppers. Expectations push them up too, since people who expect higher prices ask for bigger raises and buy sooner. Savers holding cash and retirees on a pension that never rises lose ground. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain, since they repay in dollars that buy less, and workers whose raises keep pace hold their own.

In a recent development, prices rose about 92% from January 2000 to December 2025, by the government’s Consumer Price Index. By the end, $10,000 left in a checking account that paid no interest bought only what about $5,200 bought in 2000, as the BLS’s CPI Inflation Calculator shows. Interest shrinks that loss, but only a rate above inflation, a positive real interest rate, adds buying power. So sort your money by when you’ll spend it.

According to recent reports, keep your emergency fund and money you’ll need within five years in a high-yield savings account, where it earns interest and can’t drop with stock prices. Invest the rest in low-cost index funds, which own hundreds or thousands of stocks at once, through your 401(k), an individual retirement account (IRA), or a brokerage account.

In a recent development, with dividends reinvested and before fees and taxes, $10,000 invested in the S&P 500, an index of 500 large U.S. companies, grew to about $73,900 over those years, by our math from NYU professor Aswath Damodaran’s return data. That $73,900 bought what about $38,500 bought in 2000, despite a 37% loss in 2008, which is why only money you can leave alone for years belongs in stocks.

Total your emergency fund and the next five years of planned spending, keep that much in savings, and invest every dollar beyond it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a family trip of three nights or more, compare a hotel suite, extended-stay room, or rental with a kitchen to a standard room. Add up the kitchen’s extra cost for the whole stay, any cleaning fee included, and book the one with the kitchen if cooking breakfast and a few dinners would save your family more than that.

It has been revealed that that extra cost highlights up in the nightly rate. The savings show up at every meal your family doesn’t buy at a restaurant.

Sources indicate that say a room with a kitchen costs your family of four $30 a night more than one without. Breakfast out costs $50 and dinner $100, against $15 and $30 for the same meals from a grocery store. Cooking breakfast saves $35 a day, which covers the $30 on its own.

Industry observers note that over five nights, cooking every breakfast and two dinners saves $315, or $165 after the kitchen’s extra $150. On a stay of a night or two, the kitchen often doesn’t pay off, because some costs come once per stay, such as the coffee, oil, and spices from your first grocery run. A rental’s cleaning fee is one of them. A $100 fee adds $50 a night to a two-night stay, more than the $35 a day you save by cooking breakfast, but only $20 a night to a five-night one.

Extended-stay chains put a kitchen in every room. Extended Stay America’s suites all have full kitchens, and the chain discounts longer stays. Candlewood Suites’ studios and suites come with full kitchens too. Some extended-stay chains also serve a free breakfast, so there the kitchen saves you money only on the other meals you cook. Check for a stovetop, since some kitchenettes have only a microwave.

Sources indicate that on Airbnb or Vrbo, compare a rental’s total price for your dates with a hotel’s. Under the Federal Trade Commission’s fee rule, that total must include the cleaning fee, as a hotel’s must include any resort fee, though taxes can be added before you pay.

In a recent development, shop on day one for breakfasts and two or three dinners that share ingredients, such as taco meat one night and burrito bowls the next. Plan a dinner out every day or two so nobody spends the trip at the stove.

If cooking breakfast saves your family more than the kitchen’s extra cost per night, with any cleaning fee divided across your nights, the kitchen pays for itself before you cook a single dinner.

Industry News: Unlimited Phone Data – Check Your Heaviest Month Before You Pay for It

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (494 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that before you pay for unlimited phone data, check how much cellular data you actually use.
  • Data your phone uses on Wi-Fi at home and at work never counts against your plan.
  • Start with your carrier’s count, since a data cap is measured against it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that before you pay for unlimited phone data, check how much cellular data you actually use. Your carrier’s app or past bills show it month by month, and if your heaviest recent month, hotspot included, fits under a cheaper plan with a data cap, switch to that plan and keep the difference.

Data your phone uses on Wi-Fi at home and at work never counts against your plan. If you’re on Wi-Fi most of the day, your phone may use only a few gigabytes of cellular data a month.

Start with your carrier’s count, since a data cap is measured against it. Its app or online account shows each line’s use by billing cycle, as do past bills, so look back three to six months to catch any heavy month.

Your phone’s settings show which apps used the data. On an iPhone, the Current Period total in Settings > Cellular counts all data since the last time anyone tapped Reset Statistics on that screen, so tap it on the day your billing cycle starts. On an Android phone, you can set the data usage cycle to start on your billing date.

Size the initiative to your heaviest month, not your average, and make sure that month includes any hotspot use, which some carriers list separately. Then check whether a capped plan counts hotspot data against its monthly allowance or leaves hotspot out, as some cheap plans do.

Sources indicate that take a commuter whose carrier’s app shows about 6 GB in a typical month and 9 GB in her heaviest. She pays $65 a month for an unlimited line whose extras she wouldn’t miss. Switching to a prepaid initiative with 15 GB on the same network, at $25 a month, covers her heaviest month and saves her $480 a year.

Going past a prepaid plan’s allowance usually slows your data or pauses it until you buy more, rather than adding a charge. The plan’s broadband label, a fact sheet the FCC requires for every plan, has to say which. Unlimited is worth paying for if you stream video away from Wi-Fi most days, often use your phone as a hotspot, take video calls on the road, or have a family whose data use swings from month to month.

Choose a plan whose allowance clears your heaviest month by a few gigabytes.

I was happy with this fun fresh way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,.

Sources indicate that “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

According to recent reports, okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

Sources indicate that so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

It has been revealed that admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

Sources indicate that I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Industry observers note that then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It has been revealed that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Industry observers note that experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

According to recent reports, one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

Recent findings suggest that so I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Industry observers note that thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

According to recent reports, so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

Recent findings suggest that but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Breaking: Travel in the Shoulder Season – Price the Same Trip Week by Week

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Move your trip into the destination’s shoulder season, the weeks just before or after its peak, and the same flights often cost less, with thinner crowds and weather that’s usually still good.
  • The biggest savings are usually in the airfare.
  • When schools are in session, fewer families travel, so airlines cut fares to fill seats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Move your trip into the destination’s shoulder season, the weeks just before or after its peak, and the same flights often cost less, with thinner crowds and weather that’s usually still good. The discount varies by place and year, so compare prices for several weeks around your dates before you book.

The biggest savings are usually in the airfare. Data from the travel app Hopper, reported by CNBC, highlights round-trip flights from the U.S. to Europe costing 22% less, on average, in fall 2026 than that summer.

When schools are in session, fewer families travel, so airlines cut fares to fill seats. Retirees, remote workers, and parents of kids too young for school can travel then.

The discount isn’t automatic, though. The same data puts average U.S. domestic fares for fall 2026 just above summer’s. And Expedia found that lodging in the 10 U.S. destinations most searched on its site cost 20% more, on average, in fall 2026 than in summer.

Start by finding when your destination’s peak falls. In much of Europe it’s summer, so look at April or October. In the Caribbean, the peak runs from mid-December to mid-April. Try late April through June, before hurricane season’s most active stretch from mid-August to mid-October. Or go in early December, after the season ends Nov. 30.

Expect trade-offs. Some attractions shorten their hours or close for the season, and the weather is less predictable than at peak. For a trip during hurricane season, buy travel insurance before a storm is named, since a policy bought later likely won’t cover that storm.

Then price the trip week by week. Google Flights’ price graph highlights a route’s fares by week, so compare your first-choice dates with two or three shoulder weeks, and check hotel rates for the same weeks. Say a couple’s round-trip tickets to Rome cost $1,000 each in July. At Hopper’s 22% average, mid-October tickets would cost about $780 each, $440 less for the pair than in July.

In a recent development, book the shoulder week whenever its flights and room together cost no more than those for your first-choice dates. At the same price, you still get the thinner crowds.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How soon your tax refund arrives depends on how you file.
  • Two filers who finish error-free returns on the same February day, neither claiming a credit that by law delays the refund, can get their refunds weeks apart.
  • Industry observers note that the one who e-files with direct deposit typically has the money within three weeks, according to the IRS’s Where’s My Refund page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How soon your tax refund arrives depends on how you file. E-file and choose direct deposit, and the IRS typically pays within three weeks, while a mailed paper return takes six weeks or more. Double-check your routing and account numbers, since missing or rejected bank details can now put your refund on hold.

Two filers who finish error-free returns on the same February day, neither claiming a credit that by law delays the refund, can get their refunds weeks apart.

Industry observers note that the one who e-files with direct deposit typically has the money within three weeks, according to the IRS’s Where’s My Refund page. The one who mails a paper return can’t see the refund’s status there for four weeks and should expect the refund six weeks or more after the IRS receives the return.

Industry observers note that even an e-filed refund can take longer or come in smaller. By law, the IRS can’t issue a refund before mid-February when the return claims the earned income tax credit or the additional child tax credit, and the hold covers the whole refund. A math error or a forgotten signature can delay a refund too. If the IRS mails you a letter asking you to verify your identity, such as Letter 5071C, it won’t finish processing your return until you do. And a past-due debt such as child support can take part or all of the refund.

The IRS began phasing out paper refund checks on Sept. 30, 2025, so the bank account you list on your return now matters as much as e-filing. Leave it off, or enter numbers the bank rejects, and the IRS will likely hold the refund and mail you a CP53E notice asking for a bank account. You have 30 days, and a single try, to add it through your IRS online account, and the IRS usually pays within seven days of that patch. Let the 30 days pass, and a paper check goes out six weeks after the notice.

So e-file with direct deposit, and copy your account number and your bank’s routing number from its app or online banking.

Then check Where’s My Refund or the IRS app, which replaced IRS2Go, starting about 24 hours after you e-file. Both update once a day, usually overnight, so checking more often indicates nothing new.

Install the eSIM over Wi-Fi at home, then switch it on when you land, with data roaming on for that line only.

Industry observers note that A local SIM card bought on arrival works too, but not in an iPhone 14 or later bought in the U.S., which takes only an eSIM. A day pass still makes sense for a trip of a day or two, since it keeps your own number working with nothing to install.

Turning off data roaming on your U.S. line keeps background apps from setting off a $12 day pass, but calls and texts still can. On AT&T, making or answering one call or sending one text abroad adds the pass automatically, as Verizon does on its Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Welcome prepares. Call and text through WhatsApp or FaceTime instead.

Recent findings suggest that say a household pays $10 a month for an unused watch line, $13 for insurance on a paid-off phone, and $5 for an international add-on. Canceling all three saves $28 a month, plus the per-line fee and taxes on the watch line.

#79473. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2747 w)

My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

Industry observers note that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

Industry observers note that but a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Recent findings suggest that long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

In a recent development, another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

Industry observers note that the next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

Recent findings suggest that and wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

Sources indicate that it turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In a recent development, in many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

It has been revealed that but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

Industry observers note that while this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

According to recent reports, distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

Industry observers note that but on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Recent findings suggest that since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a newly introduced, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

In a recent development, when you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that claims, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

It has been revealed that the modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Sources indicate that since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

It has been revealed that many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

According to recent reports, more modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

In a recent development, and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

Sources indicate that the great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The tech giant that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

It has been revealed that note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

In the Comments: Do you have questions about hormone replacement or anything else in this article? I’ll try to invite Kevin, Dr. Sean Bender and other knowledgeable people to contribute and answer questions as well.

Sources indicate that before you blueprint an early exit from work, read two or three of the books behind the financial independence movement, one for the investing math, one for how you think about money, and one on the path you’d take. Borrow them from the library first, and favor authors who invest in low-cost funds over ones selling a shortcut.

A forum thread on FIRE, short for financial independence, retire early, gives you one stranger’s spreadsheet. A book gives you a whole initiative and the reasoning behind it, so you can see where it fits your life and where it doesn’t.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t need all eight. A book on the math indicates how much saving and investing it takes to leave work early, one on the mindset helps you keep at it for years, and one on a single path shows what those years look like. One of each gives you a initiative to test instead of a pile of tips.

According to recent reports, judge any FIRE book you find later by how its author invests. A proposal built on low-cost index funds, which own every stock in a market index, has nothing extra to sell you. One that only works with the author’s course, coaching, or trading system is selling a shortcut.

The eight below start with the math and the mindset, move on to five different paths, and end with a counterpoint on spending.

For more on investing itself, a few investing books for beginners go deeper on index funds, investor behavior, and stock picking.

Industry observers note that before you buy any of them, check what your library card covers, since thousands of libraries lend e-books and audiobooks free through apps such as Libby and hoopla. Then test whichever plan wins you over against your own numbers, starting with your savings rate, before you change anything at work.

Kitchen or Bath Remodel – The Cheapest Layout Is the One You Already Have

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that moving a sink, toilet, or shower is one of the priciest changes in a kitchen or bath remodel, since upcoming drain, vent, and supply lines mean opening floors and walls, paying a licensed plumber, and pulling permits.
  • Fixtures cost the same wherever they sit, so the money a latest layout adds goes into pipes you’ll never see.
  • Sources indicate that drains run on gravity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that moving a sink, toilet, or shower is one of the priciest changes in a kitchen or bath remodel, since upcoming drain, vent, and supply lines mean opening floors and walls, paying a licensed plumber, and pulling permits. Leave each fixture on the drain it uses now, and spend your budget on what you see instead.

Fixtures cost the same wherever they sit, so the money a latest layout adds goes into pipes you’ll never see.

Sources indicate that drains run on gravity. The International Residential Code, the model code for houses, requires a sink’s or shower’s drain to drop at least a quarter inch for every foot it runs. Over 12 feet, that’s at least 3 inches of drop the floor has to make room for. Each fixture also needs a vent pipe nearby, so a long move can mean running a new one up through a wall.

The toilet is the hardest to move, since its drain must be at least 3 inches wide. Under a wood floor, rerouting that pipe can mean cutting and reinforcing joists. On a concrete slab, the floor has to be cut open and patched for any move.

It has been revealed that so change what you see and leave the pipes where they are. A newly introduced toilet fits the old drain when it matches the rough-in, the distance from the wall to the drain’s center. A vanity, counters, tile, lighting, and paint all go in around the pipes you have. The same code’s list of work exempt from permits includes painting, tile, cabinets, and countertops. A relocated drain or supply pipe needs a permit and an inspection before the walls close.

It has been revealed that say a bid for a slab-floor bathroom adds $9,500 to put the toilet and a newly introduced shower on the far wall. Leaving the toilet alone and setting the shower in the tub’s spot, on a base made to drain where the tub did, keeps that $9,500 for the parts you see.

Move a fixture only when the layout fails you every day, like a kitchen sink with no counter beside it. Even then, keep the move to a few feet, toward the existing drain and vent.

Before you sign, have every bidder price the job twice, with each fixture where it is and with your upcoming layout, so you see what the move alone costs.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That noted, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like fresh credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most key concerns for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

In a recent development, generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Recent findings suggest that most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

It has been revealed that one step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In a recent development, in fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Sources indicate that some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit rapidly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

Industry observers note that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an concern with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

Industry observers note that college students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

Ground Ambulance Bill – The No Surprises Act Won’t Cap It, but Your State Might

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the No Surprises Act protects you from surprise air ambulance bills but not ground ambulance bills.
  • With private insurance, the No Surprises Act keeps an air ambulance from charging you more than an in-network one would, as long as your plan covers emergency care.
  • It has been revealed that people in 22 states had some protection from surprise ground ambulance bills as of February 2026, the Commonwealth Fund found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the No Surprises Act protects you from surprise air ambulance bills but not ground ambulance bills. Before you pay a ground ambulance bill, check whether your state caps it, make sure your insurer processed the ride as an emergency, and ask the ambulance service for a discount or payment strategy.

With private insurance, the No Surprises Act keeps an air ambulance from charging you more than an in-network one would, as long as your plan covers emergency care. What you owe a ground ambulance depends on your state’s law, which may cap the bill at what an in-network ambulance would charge you.

It has been revealed that people in 22 states had some protection from surprise ground ambulance bills as of February 2026, the Commonwealth Fund found. But states can’t regulate self-funded employer prepares, where the employer pays claims from its own funds, and 71% of workers with job-based coverage are in such a plan, according to KFF’s 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey.

It has been revealed that say your state limits you to what an in-network ride would cost and your blueprint’s in-network ambulance copay is $150. A $1,800 bill for the part your insurer didn’t pay then drops to $150.

Ask your state insurance department whether a state law covers your ride and your plan. Your HR office, or the number on your insurance card, can tell you whether the plan is self-funded.

Next, check the bill against your explanation of benefits, the statement your insurer sends showing what it paid and what you owe. If the insurer denied the claim or processed the ride as a nonemergency, ask it to process the claim again as an emergency, and appeal in writing if it won’t.

Sources indicate that then call the ambulance service’s billing office to negotiate the bill. Many ambulance services are part of a fire department or a government agency. A federal advisory committee reported in 2024 that some public services, including those in Baltimore and Baton Rouge, waive patients’ share of the bill for emergency rides.

Ask whether the service cuts charges for residents or for financial hardship, and for a payment strategy on whatever is left. Every step here can wait until after the ride, so never let worry about a bill delay a 911 call.

Breaking: Missed the Tax Deadline? File Now – The Penalty Grows Monthly Without a Clean Record

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re owed a refund, there’s no penalty, but file within three years of the deadline or lose it.
  • Sources indicate that say you don’t qualify for that waiver, pay nothing until you file, and owe $4,000.
  • Of that, $900 is the late-filing penalty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

File your late tax return now. If you’re owed a refund, there’s no penalty, but file within three years of the deadline or lose it. If you owe, the penalty is 5% of the unpaid tax a month, up to 25%, though the IRS waives it automatically if you filed and paid on time the three prior years.

Sources indicate that say you don’t qualify for that waiver, pay nothing until you file, and owe $4,000. File five months late, and the penalties reach $1,000, a quarter of the bill, before interest.

Of that, $900 is the late-filing penalty. Paying late costs 0.5% of the unpaid tax a month, and when both apply, the IRS trims the filing penalty by that amount, so together they come to 5% a month. File within a month of the deadline instead, and the penalties come to $200, plus $20 for each month the tax then stays unpaid.

Once you’re more than 60 days late, the filing penalty is at least $525 or the full tax due, whichever is less, so on a small balance the penalty can match the tax itself.

Industry observers note that the waiver is the IRS’s Automatic Exemption from Penalty. On a 2025 or later return, the IRS doesn’t charge either penalty as long as you filed and paid on time for the three prior years. It applies when the IRS processes the return, and a letter confirms it, so there’s nothing to request. Without that record, you can still ask the IRS to remove a penalty for reasonable cause, such as a fire, a serious illness, or a death in the family. Neither one removes the interest, which runs on unpaid tax from the April deadline and builds daily until you pay.

So file now, even if you can’t pay it all. Filing stops the 5% penalty from growing, and interest stops on every dollar you pay.

Pay what you can through IRS Direct Pay, which draws the payment from your bank account for free, and set up an IRS payment initiative for the rest.
